title_original: At 96, Surrealist Painter Cossette Zeno Is Finally Having Her Moment
excerpt_original: While most people are sleeping, the Puerto Rican artist is painting late into the night.

blocks.text: “This one over here is a weird one,” said Cossette Zeno , pointing to her 1952 painting Let’s Go Higher . Produced while she was still a student at the University of Puerto Rico in San Juan, the painting is a true oddity. It features an array of cubes in a largely vacant landscape set beneath a haze. A set of tiny people climb these angular modules, most of which have no windows or obvious function.

We met at Richard Saltoun’s New York gallery, where she is currently the subject of a small survey of her work from the 1950s. There, she drew my attention to the only cube depicted with a doorway in Let’s Go Higher . The green structure resembles a storage container emanating light. A single figure stands atop the cube proudly gesturing toward everything else around him. “He’s saying, ‘Always up, never down,’” Zeno said with a smile.
It’s an apt description of Zeno’s career, which spans nearly a century yet evaded global recognition until the past few years.

Zeno, 96, figured memorably in two major Surrealism surveys—one presenting a globalized version of the movement , which appeared at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Tate Modern between 2021 and 2022, and another exploring its Caribbean strain , which showed at the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth in Texas in 2024. Her latest showing, the Richard Saltoun show, is on view through Friday.

links.text: a globalized version of the movement

blocks.text: During the ’50s, Zeno forged a connection with André Breton, a cofounder of Surrealism, and exhibited alongside the movement’s adherents in Europe. Yet she never received canonization, perhaps because of her gender or because of the limited geographic focus of many Western art historians. Plus, as the scholar Whitney Chadwick has pointed out, many female Surrealists did not identify as members of the movement, in part because they felt alienated by their male counterparts. This sense of marginalization sidelined painters such as Meret Oppenheim, Leonora Carrington, and Remedios Varo, all of whom are now considered essential to Surrealist art history .
When I asked how she identified, however, she told me, “I call myself a Surrealist because I have their spirit of freedom. I have no fences. I am always evolving, baby!”

blocks.alt: A painting of a tangle of corporeal forms with tufts of hair on top.
blocks.caption: Cossette Zeno, Ni hablar del peluquín (No Use to Talk about the Little Wig …) , 1952. Courtesy Richard Saltoun

blocks.text: Her Surrealist spirit is abundantly evident in Ni hablar del peluquín (No Use to Talk about the Little Wig), the 1952 painting that featured in both institutional surveys. The painting features a monstrous tangle of flesh, with snatches of hair that might belong either to the titular toupee or to a more risqué part of the body.
“That represents a guy,” Zeno said. Nodding to the painting’s overt eroticism, she continued, “He’s thinking many things—you can decide what he’s thinking. He has a toupee, so he’s not a young guy.”

Male Surrealists like Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, and René Magritte were known for depicting the nude female body as a locus of desire and intrigue. Zeno, by contrast, estimated that she had only ever painted one naked woman. Why? “I like men,” she quipped.

Taking sips of beer, Zeno told me that works like this one were produced late at night. Still today, she’ll begin work at 11 p.m. and go to bed at 7 a.m. “Everybody who could bother me would be sleeping,” she said. “I’m free from cooking. I don’t have to clean the house.”

Many Surrealists likened their work to dreams, and that makes it notable that Zeno creates her work when others are in the REM stage of sleep. (This recalls a phrase once used by the Cuban Surrealist painter Wifredo Lam: “When I don’t sleep, I dream.”) Of her late-night art-making, Zeno told me, “I’m fully aware of what I’m doing.”

blocks.alt: A painting of vine-like forms set against a green background.
blocks.caption: Cossette Zeno, Tropical Haze , 1954. Photo Charles Roussel

blocks.text: Zeno was born in the Dominican Republic in 1930, not long after the dictator Rafael Leónidas Trujillo seized power following a period of upheaval. When she was a toddler, Zeno and her family went into exile and left for Puerto Rico. “I don’t know Santo Domingo at all,” Zeno said. “That’s why I call myself Puerto Rican.”

In Old San Juan, Zeno took a liking to the mountains and sea all around her. “No matter where you stand in Puerto Rico, you see the ocean,” she said. “My grandmother used to take me to the ocean at 6 o’clock in the morning, so that I could see the little fish caught in the bubbles. I used to snorkel all the time.” Later, she added, “I’m very close to nature.”

Some of her earliest works reflect that. Two oil crayon drawings feature a mix of swirling white forms; they could represent shells tumbling through a current. (Zeno made them on paper she procured from her father’s business.) Tropical Haze (1954) features vine-like lines running through a greenish background, and it’s not hard to imagine they’re based on greenery Zeno encountered firsthand.

blocks.alt: A painting showing a boat passing beneath an arch of diamonds.
blocks.caption: Cossette Zeno, Safe Journey , 1951. Photo Charles Roussel

blocks.text: She entered the University of Puerto Rico at a time of profound change for the island. A series of revolts against the US military in 1950 helped galvanize the Puerto Rican nationalist spirit, and artists were enlisted to advance the spirit of self-determination.

Under the tutelage of Eugenio Granell, a Spanish Surrealist whose leftist politics had driven him to from Europe to the Caribbean during World War II, Zeno struck out in a different direction from other Puerto Rican artists, encoding her messages about the fight for independence in the visual language of Surrealism. She pointed to Safe Journey (1951), a painting in which a boat sails beneath a diamond arch. That arch, she said, signifies that “Puerto Rico is a poor country, but it’s not poor.” A fearsome beast reaches out to strike the boat, but it is blind, and so, she said, “there’s no threat. It has no power.”

After graduating from the University of Puerto Rico in 1953, Zeno received a postgraduate scholarship to study at the École du Louvre in Paris. There, she met Breton, whose influentialwas so great that she named one of her daughters after his 1928 book Nadja .

blocks.alt: A woman standing beneath two abstract drawings.
blocks.caption: Cossette Zeno at her Richard Saltoun show. Courtesy Richard Saltoun

blocks.text: Her parents were living in Cuba at the time, and her father’s illness called her back to the Caribbean in 1954. More upheaval followed. She recalled being forced to leave Cuba twice. Once, while working for a textile company, she encountered a man bleeding out in the street and ran back to her job, where she warned a coworker of the reach of Fulgencio Batista’s regime; the employee ended up being a secret agent who urged her to leave Cuba expediently. Later, after marrying in the United States, she returned to visit her parents during the Castro era, only to find herself uprooted once more when he changed Cuba’s currency in 1961, rendering her money worthless.

Zeno has moved frequently over the years and is now based in Jackson, Missouri, where her granddaughter lives. She has never maintained a studio, she said, and there have been periods when she stopped painting altogether, including the year that her husband, Robert Bates, died.

blocks.alt: A painting of a stack of cubes, some of which are linked by small pipes. Tiny figures can be seen atop them.
blocks.caption: Cossette Zeno, Let’s Go Higher , 1952. Courtesy Richard Saltoun

blocks.text: But she is still working, and she excitedly told me about a new project: a painting spread across four full-size doors. Her grandson had initially asked her to paint a mural for the Atlanta hotel he’s opening, but she took the idea in a different direction. Working on the floor, Zeno is painting the doors with what she described as “sea elements.” This December, the doors will travel to Richard Saltoun’s booth at the Untitled Art, Miami Beach fair.

Her use of the doors recalls the portal in Let’s Go Higher , the painting with the unusually colored cubes. At one point in our interview, she reiterated her interpretation of the work: “You never go down, always up.”
